HERBERT LAWRENCE BRIDGMAN, GAMMA '66
Editor's Note At the request of the Executive Council we merely announce

Brother Bridgman's death, in this issue. The January number will be dedicated to his
memory and wiU contain many interesting articles, and a detailed report of the memorial
exercises to be held in New York on Founders Day, November 24th.

L.
BRIDGMAN, president of the Executive Council, famous
HERBERT
explorer, Regent of the University of the State of New York and
business manager of The Standard Union, died Wednesday, September 24th,
in mid-Atlantic aboard the State schoolship Newport.

Although 80 years of age, Mr. Bridgman had been in excellent health
up to the moment of his death. His home was at 604 Carlton Avenue,
Brooklyn, New York.
The radio message from Capt. Reisenberg, which came as a totally
unexpected shock to Brooklynites, read as follows:
Radiogram
"Radio Corporation of America. Received at 64 Broad Street, New York,
Sept. 26, 1924, 1:51 A.M.
"Schoolship Newport (NMH) Standard Union.
"Brooklyn, N. Y.
"Regent Herbert L. Bridgman died six-fifteen morning, Sept. 24. Lat.
29 degrees 44 minutes north; Ion. 56 degrees 32 minutes west.
"Death sudden after slight illness. Was attended by ship's surgeon.
Dr. Kelly. Captain and surgeons were present at time of death; result of
sudden stroke and hemorrhage. He died without pain.

"Regent Bridgman was on deck enjoying fine weather the day before
his death. He was in high spirits and spoke of many activities he had in
mind on his return. This was his first illness on the cruise. His health
seemed good just before his death.
"His papers and valuables have been sealed by a Board of Inventory.
His body was wrapped in sheets and placed in the refrigerator room. It
will be embalmed. A metallic coffin has been ordered.

"Regent Bridgman had endeared himself to all on board. A general
muster was called at noon after his death. The ship was
stopped for ten
minutes, ensign and pennant half-masted and a prayer was read.
"Then proceeded full speed to Hamilton, Bermuda. Will arrive Fri
day; leave for New York Saturday. Expect arrive via Sandy Hook Tues
day. Will radio exact time.
"Guard of honor has been placed by the remains since time of death.
Cadet guard will be ready to render honors on arrival.

"Riesenberg."

While a bugler from the training ship Newport sounded
taps the body
of Dr. Herbert L. Bridgman was laid to rest in Greenwood Cemetery, New
York, on October 1st. The funeral services were held in the afternoon at
the Church of the Pilgrims, Henry and Remsen Streets, Brooklyn, and
more than 1,000 persons gathered to
pay a last tribute to Dr. Bridgman.
The services were conducted by the Rev. Dr. Howard Dean French,
life-long friend of the late publisher, while fifty cadets from the New York
Schoolship Newport acted as guard of honor.
In his eulogy Dr. French described Dr. Bridgman as an adventurer in
the service of mankind. He said that he had been a man of great character
and one who would be difficult to replace. "Abide With Me" was sung by
Miss Emma L. Jones, of The Standard Union.
His body was taken under guard from the ship to his former home at
604 Carlton Avenue, Brooklyn. The cadets lined the street as the body was
carried into the church and at the conclusion of the services they again
formed as a guard and escorted the coffin to the cemetery.
Among those who attended the services were the Executive Council in
a body, together with former members, Waugh,
Whiting, Wertheimer and
Keppel. The Gamma, Delta and Lambda Chapters also sent representa
tives. The two United States Senators from New York Wadsworth and

Copeland also attended, as well as Mayor Hylan; Charles Dodd, District

Attorney of Kings; Sheriff John N. Harmon; Borough President Edward
Riegelmann ; John F. McCooey, Democratic county leader, and Jacob Living
ston, Republican county leader; former Senator Charles A. Lockwood; for
mer United States Senator William M. Calder ; former State Senator William
Heffernan; Gerhard M. Dahl, President of the B. M. T., and Arthur S.
Somers, a Director of the B. M. T. and President of the Brooklyn Chamber
of Commerce; Federal Judge Robert Inch; Magistrates Francis McCloskey,
Louis Reynolds and Hyman Rayfield; Herbert F. Gunnison, Arthur M.
Howe, Raymond Gunnison and James M. Wood of The Brooklyn Eagle;
John A. Halton, T. Bossard and Joseph J. Early of The Brooklyn Standard
Union, and Edward C. Blum.
There were present M. Stephen Panaretoff, Minister from Bulgaria to
the United States, and his staff, who came from Washington in recognition
of Dr. Bridgman's efforts in organizing the educational system of their
country.
Among the organizations represented at the church were the Publishers'
Association of New York City, Sons of the Revolution, the Explorers' Club,
the American Newspaper Publishers' Association, the Peary Arctic Club,
the American, National and Philadelphia Geographical Societies, the Amer
ican Alpine Club, the Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences, the New
York State University, Amherst College Alumni Association, the Brooklyn
Chamber of Commerce and the Board of Education.

the Executive Council held a meeting on October 21st and unanimously
elected Brother Earl D. Babst to the office of President of the Executive
Council.
The news of the selection of Brother Babst will prove most welcome
to alumni and undergraduates, for he will be a worthy successor to

Brother Bridgman.
Brother Babst has been a member of the Executive Council continuously
since 1907 with the exception of one year, and his counsel has been of
great weight and value to the fraternity. His election proved to be a sur
prise to him, for in his modesty he had never thought of himself being
selected for this high office. After his election he wrote to one of his
associates on the Council saying, "I find myself somewhat under the spell
of the honor and responsibility I assumed Tuesday evening! No one had
spoken to me in advance. Naturally, I will do all I can to meet your

expectations and trust, but shall lean very heavily on you and the others."
Brother Babst will not have a moment's anxiety in his new role as
President of the Council, for all of the Chapters and alumni will rally
to his leadership and look forward to the future with confidence in his

ability and judgment to lead us on to greater accomplishments than even
our noble past.
Earl D. Babst is president of the American Sugar Refining Company.
He entered the Fraternity in 1889 as a nineteen year old Iota freshman,
and graduated in 1893 from the Phi with a Bachelor of Philosophy degree
in his pocket and a Phi Beta Kappa key on his watch chain. He was
admitted to the Michigan bar in 1894, and after practicing in Detroit for
eight years, he became a member of Green, Peters & Babst, of Chicago,
general counsel of the National Biscuit, American Radiator and other cor
porations, removing in 1905 to New York and becoming general counsel
and later first vice-president of the Biscuit Company. In 1911 Michigan
gave him an honorary master of arts
degree. In 1915 he was elected presi

dent of the American Sugar and represented the United States during the
war in the allocation of
sugar supplies to the Allies. He is a director of
the Metropolitan and Mercantile Trust Companies and Great American,
American Alliance, and Massachusetts Fire and Marine Insurance Com
panies; was president of the University of Michigan Club, 1912-13; of the
Kenyon Alumni Association 1915-17. Since 1907, he has been a member
of the Michigan Alumni Advisory Council. Brother Babst was married in
1903 to Edwina Uhl, daughter of the late Edwin F. Uhl, American Ambas
sador to Germany.

OMICRON CHAPTER MOVES INTO ITS NEW HOME

chapter at the University of Illinois moved into its new home
OUR
this fall.
Located on the soutwest corner of Fourth Street and Armory Avenue,
it is placed on the lot with its quarter circle facade facing the corner
so that the front, east and north walls combine to make the principal
elevation, and the long front so produced combines pleasingly with the
great elm on the corner as seen from the principal approach.
As you approach the house, you see a broad expanse of lawn with
the building set well back from the street and planted so as to force
entrance well back from the corner on either street.
The mass and outline of the building develop a natural, rather
than contrived picturesqueness. The style shows the same spirit which
animated the Sixteenth Century Englishman, when he built in native style
and period. Precisely the same careful attention to line and proportion,
and right adaptation of features to their purposes are apparent through
out the building.
The front is dominated by two large chimneys and centered between
them on the axis of the lot and circle is the main entrance of stone. This
feature rises to a height above the second story window sills, where it
is topped by the Ancient Owl, and because it is symbolic, it becomes the
main feature of the exterior of the building.
The materials used chiefly for the walls are a rough textured brick
which will be treated with a special whitewash. The window lintels are
of stone, as are also the porch piers of the living porch on the south.
Entering the house through the vestibule, you enter a circular gal
lery from which easy oak stairs rise to the second floor. The gallery is
treated with heavy wooden ceiling beams and openings cased with heavy
timbers, framed and nail-studded in the English manner. Flanking the
main entrance doors two recesses are formed and the space thus obtained
is occupied by upholstered seats.
Opening naturally from each end of the gallery are the living room
on the east and the dining room on the north. These rooms are alike
in size and similar in treatment, with rough plastered walls, brick fire
places, brick and masonry window openings. The great recessed fire
place in the living room occupies more than half of the north wall of
this room. Recesses formed in walls in the living room and dining room
provide space for chests and the display of various trophies.
These rooms with the gallery form practically one room for pur
poses of entertaining. To the south of the living room are a glazed living
porch and a library.
On the south wall of the gallery and east of the main stair a door
opens into a large coat room, in which are located telephone booths, coat

tangible

Editor's Note The following article by Brother White is the second of what we

expect to be a regular contribution to each issue of the Diamond. True our Chapter at
Harvard is not active as is well known, but its illustrious and loyal Alumni merit frequent
mention in our columns and we feel proud to have Brother Horatio Stevens White as
our permanent Associate Editor. He is Professor of German at Harvard.

later Alpha, 1870-73, numbered 63 members, of the classes of '71,
THE'72, '73, '74, and '75. The present year (1924) twenty-four of these
were still surviving, a goodly percentage for graduates of half a century's
standing. Although the record of the later Alphans was not so brilliant
nor so varied as that of the earlier group, the learned professions, especially
law and medicine, were well represented among them. Perhaps the most
distinguished of Boston surgeons was Dr. M. H. Richardson of '73, Moseley
Professor of Surgery in the Harvard Medical School, beloved by hundreds
of grateful patients, dying prematurely in 1912.

Other well-known Boston physicians were George Stedman, '71 (de
ceased) and H. R. Stedman, '71 (retired). Samuel Brearley, '71, was the
founder of the successful Day School for Girls in New York City. A. L.
Lincoln, Class Secretary of '72, Park Commissioner, is a Boston lawyer.
L. C. Ledyard, '72, is a prominent lawyer and financier in New York.
Another Psi Upsilon surgeon is O. H. Everett, '73, of Worcester, Mass.
A. L. Ware, '73, son of Rev. J. F. W. Ware, was for nearly fifty years
the faithful secretary of his class.
H. S. White, '73, has been a professor and dean at Cornell University
and is now a professor emeritus of Harvard. He is co-executor with Ira A.
Place (Chi, '81, and vice-president of the New York Central Railroad, in
charge of the Law Department) , of the estate of Willard Fiske, Psi, '51. As
literary executor, the former is at present engaged in preparing the "Life
and Correspondence of Willard Fiske" as a conclusion to the "Memorials,"
selections from which have already appeared in The Diamond. Of the same
class is Walter Raymond of Pasadena, California, whose organized excur
sions have given him a world-wide publicity. Another classmate, C. K.
Lexow, Commissioner of Records in New York City, is known to all mem
bers of the local Psi Upsilon Club, of which he has just been elected Presi
dent. Of '74 was George Riddle, the popular dramatic elocutionist, who
gave a brilliant rendition of King Dekipus, in staging the Greek play of
Sophocles; and another classmate was W. C. Sanger, Assistant Secretary of
War, influential in the movement to improve our National Guard.
Louis Dyer, '74, after graduation became connected with Balliol Col
lege, Oxford, dying in 1908. Of him Professor Willard Fiske once wrote:
"He won, after a severe competition, the Taylorian Scholarship, one of

Cornelius Cole, Xi '47

Cornelius Cole, Xi, '47, former United States senator and friend of
Abraham Lincoln, died at his home in Los Angeles on Nov. 3. He was

102 years and 2 months old.
The direct cause of death, physicians announced, was incipient pneu
monia, old age, and a touch of heart disease. He had been in frail
health for several months, so much so that celebration of his last birth
day was limited to members of the family at his residence.
Senator Cole had expected to vote on Nov. 4th, and during the clos
ing days of his career had expressed confidence that President Coolidge
would be returned to office. "He's a fine young fellow," Cole said.
Mr. Cole was born at Lodi, N. Y., Sept. 17, 1822 ^the year after

Napoleon's death. He remembered that during his childhood days the
depressing effects of the revolutionary war had not yet entirely passed
away, and he clearly recalled having seen soldiers who had served under
Washington in the days of '76.
The senator saw the first pony express arrive at San Francisco in
1860.
During the civil war Mr. Cole occupied a seat in the house of rep
resentatives and in 1866 was elected to the United States senate from Cali
fornia, serving until 1873.
Brother Cole was the Dean of Psi Upsilon Alumni and he returned

to Wesleyan University for the 75th anniversary of his graduation in 1922.
Afterward Senator Cole appeared once again in Washington and took
his old place in the senate, there to receive the tribute of a new generation
that was guiding the affairs of the nation.
When asked his views on prohibition a short time ago. Senator Cole
said there were times "when a good drink was an inspiration" and then 

quickly added that "even a great many articles of food contain an inspira
tion." Having used tobacco in moderation for four score years, he says he
quit its use five years ago because he believed smoking had a tendency to
interfere with his heart action.
